content: An embryo, derived from the Greek word meaning that which grows, is a multicellular diploid eukaryote in its earliest stage of development. This stage begins from the first cell division after fertilization and continues until birth, hatching, or germination. In humans, the term embryo is used from the moment of fertilization until the end of the 8th week of development, after which it is referred to as a fetus. The process of embryo development is called embryogenesis. In sexually reproducing organisms, fertilization occurs when a sperm cell fuses with an egg cell, forming a zygote. This zygote contains the complete DNA of both parents, with 50% of its genetic material inherited from each. In plants, animals, and some protists, the zygote undergoes mitotic divisions to form a multicellular organism, which is the embryo. In animals, the zygote develops into an embryo through distinct stages, including the blastula, gastrula, and organogenesis. The blastula stage is characterized by a fluid-filled cavity called the blastocoel, surrounded by a layer of cells known as blastomeres. During gastrulation, the cells of the blastula undergo coordinated processes such as division, migration, and invasion to form two (diploblastic) or three (triploblastic) germ layers. In triploblastic organisms, these germ layers are the ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The arrangement and positioning of these layers are species-specific, depending on the type of embryo. In vertebrates, a unique population of embryonic cells called the neural crest has been proposed as a fourth germ layer, playing a critical role in the evolution of head structures. During organogenesis, molecular and cellular interactions between the germ layers, combined with the cells' developmental potential, lead to the differentiation of organ-specific cell types. For instance, in neurogenesis, a subset of ectodermal cells is designated to form the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Modern developmental biology investigates the molecular mechanisms underlying various organogenesis processes, such as angiogenesis (formation of blood vessels), chondrogenesis (cartilage formation), myogenesis (muscle formation), and osteogenesis (bone formation). Generally, structures that evolved earlier in evolutionary history tend to appear earlier in embryonic development, a concept summarized by the phrase ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny. For example, the backbone, a common feature among vertebrates, is one of the earliest structures to form in vertebrate embryos. In humans, the cerebrum, the most advanced part of the brain, develops last. In plants, a seed plant embryo is part of the seed and consists of precursor tissues for the leaves, stem (hypocotyl), root (radicle), and one or more cotyledons. When the embryo begins to germinate and grow out of the seed, it is referred to as a seedling. Non-seed-producing plants, such as bryophytes and ferns, also produce embryos. In these plants, the embryo is a young plant that remains attached to the parental gametophyte. In animals, the embryo of a placental mammal is defined as the organism from the first division of the zygote (fertilized ovum) until it becomes a fetus. In humans, the embryonic stage begins with implantation in the uterus and lasts through the 8th week of development. After this stage, the organism is referred to as a fetus until birth or hatching. In human embryonic development, during weeks 1 to 3, the blastula attaches to the uterine wall (endometrium) and undergoes implantation. This process establishes connections between the mother and the embryo, including the formation of the umbilical cord. The embryo's growth centers around an axis that will develop into the spine and spinal cord. The brain, spinal cord, heart, and gastrointestinal tract begin to form. By weeks 4 to 5, the embryo produces chemicals that halt the woman's menstrual cycle. Neurogenesis begins, with brain activity detectable around the 6th week. The heart starts beating, and limb buds appear, marking the future growth of arms and legs. Organogenesis commences, and the head constitutes about half of the embryo's axial length and mass. The brain develops into five distinct regions, and vertebrae and bones begin to form. Blood circulation starts as the heart beats. During weeks 6 to 8, myogenesis and neurogenesis progress to the point where the embryo can move, and the eyes begin to form. Organogenesis and growth continue, with hair and all essential organs starting to develop. Facial features begin to take shape. By the end of the 8th week, the embryonic stage concludes, and the fetal stage begins. The status of the human embryo is a topic of ethical debate. Some bioethicists, including Christian ethicists, argue that an embryo possesses personhood. For example, Gilbert Meilaender, a professor of Christian ethics, identifies conception as the moment a new individual human being comes into existence, as the zygote's genotype is established at this point. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) defines the embryonic stage as the beginning of the developed human form.
